entities.name: Latinius Pacatus Drepanius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Latinius Pacatus Drepanius, an eminent Roman orator and panegyrist, flourished at the tumultuous close of the 4th century CE, with his most significant work delivered in 389 CE. Hailing from Gaul, likely Bordeaux, Pacatus rose to prominence as a master of classical Latin rhetoric, serving the Imperial court during a period of profound political and social transformation. His enduring significance lies in his *Panegyricus Latini Pacati Drepanii Theodosio Augusto*, a speech delivered in Rome before Emperor Theodosius I, which not only celebrated the emperor's decisive victory over the usurper Magnus Maximus but also serves as a crucial primary source for understanding the shifting power dynamics and ideological justifications of late Roman imperial rule, including the delicate balance between traditional Roman virtues and nascent Christian imperial ideology.

His career trajectory exemplifies the opportunities available to provincial elites within the Roman administration. In 389 CE, Pacatus traveled to Rome to present his panegyric to Theodosius I, a meticulously crafted address that lauded the emperor's military prowess and divine favor following his triumph at the Battle of the Save in 388 CE. This public display of loyalty and rhetorical skill earned him imperial favor, leading to his appointment as Proconsul of Africa, a prestigious administrative position that placed him in charge of a vital Roman province, responsible for its governance and grain supply to the capital.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Latinius Pacatus Drepanius's panegyric offers a critical primary source for understanding the political climate and imperial ideology of the late 4th-century Roman Empire, directly influencing our perception of Emperor Theodosius I's reign. His work showcases the enduring power of classical rhetoric in legitimizing power during a period of profound imperial transformation.
